short: Japan's first securely attested reigning empress, on the throne for thirty-five years.
full:
Suiko came to the throne in 593 after the Soga clan chief Umako, her uncle, had her predecessor Sushun murdered. She was the first woman to reign in her own right in the Japanese record, and she held the position for thirty-five years, longer than any empress regnant who followed. Government in practice ran through Umako and through her nephew Prince Shōtoku, who served as regent and to whom later tradition attributed the Seventeen Article Constitution of 604 and the twelve court ranks of 603.

Her reign made Buddhism a state concern rather than a clan enthusiasm: temples including Hōryū-ji were founded, and monks and craftsmen arrived from the Korean kingdoms. Embassies were sent to Sui China from 607, and the letter they carried addressed the Japanese sovereign as the ruler of the land of the rising sun, claiming parity with the Chinese emperor. Suiko died in 628 without naming a clear successor, and the disputed succession that followed helped bring on the Taika Reform.
